newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish children caught in dead-end conflict.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish children caught in dead-end conflict.

text.p: A lighted petrol bomb in one hand and a rock in the other, he is an enduring symbol of a street conflict that knows no end.
He wears a balaclava or sometimes brazenly discards it, not caring if the police recognise him.
As the smoke smoke clears, he becomes visible. Tousled hair and in jeans, he is a young teenager, sometimes not even that.
In Northern Ireland, children thrust themselves into a conflict created by adults.

Across the world since the province erupted in new violence on Sunday, images have flashed of youngsters on the front line of strife, pelting security forces with missiles and dancing their delight in the debris of burnt out vehicles.
Each night community leaders try to stop them but many youngsters seem inexorably drawn to a dice with death.
"I think for many of them it is excitememnt. In all parts of the world wartime brings excitement especially for young teenagers. That is a major factor," said psychologist and academic Ed Cairns.

"Some of them will be politically motivated but I suspect that here they are in a minority," said Cairns, a professor of psychology at the University of Ulster in the town of Coleraine and author of a book "Children and Political Violence".

Northern Ireland is not a place apart and child involvement in street violence is an international pattern, he said, citing child stone-throwers in the Intifada in the West Bank and Gaza and in the Black struggle against white rule in South Africa.
During vicious Northern Ireland riots youngsters taunt security forces, advancing slowly to lob stones and daring the riot police to chase after them.
When they score a hit with a stone or a petrol bomb, they are hero worshipped by their friends, who try to do the same.
"For them it's like being in a real action movie," said one social worker."

But the ritual game turns lethal when edgy police riots squads, fending off the petrol bombers of older years and with longer throws, start firing plastic bullets, or when guerrillas lurking behind the demonstrators counter with live rounds.

Among the first casualties of this week's violence sparked by a Protestant parade through a Catholic zone of Portadown were two 14-year-olds, one hit by a republican gunman, the other struck by a plastic bullet fired by troops at rioters.

Over 28 years Northern Ireland's medical authorities have tended numerous children hurt in riots, a lot of them just "in the wrong place at the wrong time" and lured by the unfolding drama outside their terraced houses.

"I think they get involved because of a fascination with conflict, a facination with violence. It is also a chance to show a bravado to their peers and to their community that they are doing something for it," said Michael Doherty, a youth worker in Londonderry, scene of some of the worst weekend rioting.
"Young people at the moment in Northern Ireland are picking up n the hurts of their community, and therefore they are a symbol of wider community problems."

In a society of competing political demands, where the Protestant majority supports continued British rule and the minority Irish Catholics want a united Ireland, he says more government aid should used to promote harmony between young people and show them an alternative to violence.
"They are not putting enought money in, and so there is limited scope for teaching young people to draw away from this this violence."
